items.title: Real and complex scalar conventions for normed spaces
Banach space
The reverse triangle inequality in a normed space
items.strategy: Apply the triangle inequality to x=(x-y)+y and y=(y-x)+x, then combine the two one-sided bounds. The 1-Lipschitz property of the norm is the same estimate rewritten as |\|x\|-\|y\||\le\|x-y\|.

items.title: Linear isometries and isometric isomorphisms
Normed subspace
A complete normed subspace is closed
items.strategy: Identify the metric induced by the restricted norm with the ambient subspace metric, then specialize the published metric theorem. The notes record that the standard approximating-sequence proof spends AC_omega when it manufactures a sequence from closure.

items.title: A closed subspace of a Banach space is Banach
items.strategy: Read the subspace with its restricted norm, identify its induced metric with the ambient subspace metric, and apply the closed-subspace direction of the published completeness theorem.

items.title: The standard product norms on a finite product of normed spaces
Vector addition and scalar multiplication are continuous in a normed space
items.strategy: For addition use \|(x+h)+(y+k)-(x+y)\|\le\|h\|+\|k\|. For scalar multiplication use \|(\lambda+\alpha)(x+h)-\lambda x\|\le|\lambda|\,\|h\|+|\alpha|(\|x\|+\|h\|). Read continuity on products through the product topology; in the complex case the scalar coordinate is measured with the published modulus convention.

items.title: The standard finite product norms are equivalent
items.strategy: Work with the explicit max, Euclidean, and sum formulas. The inequalities max\le 2\le 1\le n max are proved coordinatewise, using the Euclidean Cauchy-Schwarz estimate only for the middle comparison and not the global finite-dimensional norm-equivalence theorem.

items.title: Finite products of Banach spaces are Banach
items.strategy: Use the max product norm to read a Cauchy sequence coordinatewise. Each coordinate converges in its Banach factor, and the limit tuple is then a limit for the whole sequence. The equivalence lemma transports the result to the sum and Euclidean product norms.

items.title: Series and absolute convergence in a normed space
An absolutely convergent series has Cauchy partial sums
items.strategy: Bound the norm of a tail of partial sums by the corresponding tail of the scalar series of norms. Once the scalar tail is small, the vector tail is small too.

items.title: Series criterion for Banach spaces
items.strategy: One direction is immediate from completeness and the Cauchy lemma. For the converse, accelerate an arbitrary Cauchy sequence to a rapidly Cauchy subsequence, sum the successive differences as an absolutely convergent series, and recover convergence of the original sequence by a final triangle-inequality estimate.

items.title: Completion of a normed space
The Cauchy-class operations of a normed-space completion are well defined
items.strategy: Use the published Cauchy-sequence model of metric completion. Equivalent representatives remain equivalent after termwise addition and scalar multiplication, and the reverse triangle inequality makes (\|x_n\|) Cauchy so that \|[x_n]\|:=lim\|x_n\| exists and is representative-independent.

items.title: The metric completion of a normed space carries a unique compatible Banach-space structure
items.strategy: Equip the published Cauchy-class completion with the termwise operations and limiting norm of the previous lemma, check that the constant-sequence copy of the original space is a dense linear isometry, and inherit completeness from the published metric completion. Uniqueness comes from the dense-copy requirement: any other compatible operations agree on the dense image and hence everywhere by continuity.

items.title: Bounded linear maps extend uniquely across the completion
items.strategy: A bound \|Tx\|\le C\|x\| makes T Lipschitz, hence uniformly continuous, on the dense original copy. Apply the published metric extension theorem to obtain a unique extension into the Banach target, then prove linearity by comparing both sides on the dense image and preserve the operator bound by approximation.

items.title: Any two completions of a normed space are uniquely linearly isometric
items.strategy: Use the published uniqueness of metric completions to get the unique isometry fixing the dense original copy, then invoke the bounded-linear extension theorem on that dense linear isometry to show that the metric isometry is automatically linear.

items.title: The classical $L^p$ spaces are Banach spaces
$\ell^\infty$ is Banach for the supremum norm
items.strategy: Start with a sup-norm Cauchy sequence of bounded sequences, pass to coordinatewise Cauchy convergence, define the pointwise limit, and use the uniform tail bound to recover convergence in the supremum norm. The verification should also show the limit sequence stays bounded.

items.title: $c_0$ is Banach for the supremum norm
items.strategy: View c_0 as the subspace of \ell^\infty whose coordinates tend to 0. Prove directly that it is closed in \ell^\infty by splitting the tail estimate into one term coming from the fixed approximant and one from the uniform limit, then invoke the closed-subspace lemma.

items.title: $C_b(X)$ is Banach for the supremum norm
items.strategy: Use a uniformly Cauchy sequence of bounded continuous functions, define the pointwise limit, and keep continuity by the uniform limit theorem. Boundedness is inherited from one late term plus a uniform tail estimate, so the limit stays in C_b(X).

items.title: $C(K)$ is Banach when $K$ is compact metric
items.strategy: Every continuous function on a compact metric space is bounded, so C(K)=C_b(K) as sets. Apply the previous example after citing the extreme-value theorem for the boundedness step that compactness supplies automatically.

items.title: The finitely supported sequences form an incomplete normed space with different standard completions
items.strategy: For the supremum norm, truncate a null sequence to show c_00 is dense in c_0 and use a non-finitely-supported null sequence to witness incompleteness. For 1\le p<\infty, truncate an \ell^p sequence to get density in \ell^p. The completion identifications are then fixed by the uniqueness-of-completion corollary.

items.title: Polynomials are not complete in the supremum norm on a compact interval
items.strategy: Take the polynomial algebra inside C([a,b],R), invoke Stone-Weierstrass on compact metric spaces to get density, and use a nonpolynomial continuous limit to show the polynomial space is proper. The completion is identified with C([a,b],R) by the completion-uniqueness corollary.

items.title: Dictionary of the classical $L^p$ and $\ell^p$ Banach spaces
items.strategy: Package the earlier completion remark into a quick lookup example: L^p(\mu) is Banach for 1\le p\le\infty, \ell^p is the counting-measure case, and c_00 sits densely inside the classical sequence spaces discussed on this companion page.

items.title: An incomplete normed subspace need not be closed
items.strategy: Use c_00 inside c_0 with the supremum norm. The earlier examples already show c_0 is Banach and c_00 is dense but incomplete, so c_00 cannot be closed without contradicting the closed-subspace lemma.

items.title: Topologically equivalent metrics on a vector space need not come from equivalent norms
items.strategy: Start from any genuine norm metric d and replace it by min{d,1}. The bounded remetrisation gives the same topology, but if it came from a norm then absolute homogeneity would force unbounded distances along scalar multiples of any nonzero vector, contradicting the truncation at 1.
